# BRONCHITIS, NO BENEFIT FROM ANTIBACTERIAL THERAPY

Acute bronchitis is a clinical syndrome with a brief, self-limited pneumonia on
chest radiograph. It is accompanied by dry or productive cough lasting up to 3
weeks, is most prevalent in winter, and is primarily caused by viruses. More
than 1 in 20 people have acute bronchitis per year, with highest rates during
the winter months.  This discussion does not pertain to acute exacerbations of
chronic bronchitis, a clinical syndrome also frequently associated with viral
infection, but in which bacteria play a more important role.

Narcotic cough suppressants, expectorants, antihistamines, decongestants, and
beta 2-agonists have been used to treat patients with acute bronchitis, but
controlled trials have not clearly concluded that they are beneficial.

Empirical antibacterial therapy has repeatedly been shown to provide no benefit
for most patients.  Acute bronchitis remains one of the five most frequently
cited rationales for excessive antibiotic use in outpatients. Acute bronchitis
and other acute respiratory syndromes (otitis media, sinusitis, pharyngitis,
upper respiratory infections) account for approximately 75% of ambulatory
prescriptions in the United States.  Current guidelines, endorsed by several
national societies, including the Infectious Diseases Society of America, do not
recommend the routine use of antibiotics for uncomplicated acute bronchitis in
normal people.

If pertussis is suspected, early therapy with macrolides or tetracyclines is
indicated to prevent transmission, although the clinical findings early in
pertussis infection are indistinguishable from viral causes of bronchitis, and
the incidence of disease is very low.  Treat for pertussis only when a patient
has likely been exposed to other cases.

Asthma attacks often have symptoms resembling bronchitis.  Asthma attacks do not
benefit from antimicrobial therapy.
